title: NRG Energy Sells Gas Plants for Four Billion Dollars to Fund Buybacks
subtitle: Handing back generation assets to retire discounted stock resets the independent power trade
summary: NRG Energy agreed to sell six natural-gas power plants to LS Power for four billion dollars in cash while posting a sharp third-quarter earnings beat. The transaction funds three billion dollars in share repurchases as independent power producers pivot from accumulating generation capacity to returning capital.

bodyHtml:
When you open your monthly electric bill, you are almost certainly paying a retail middleman who buys electricity from someone else and tacks on a fee.

NRG Energy operates as both the landlord and the meter reader. The Houston-based utility sells electricity, natural gas, and Vivint smart-home systems to roughly eight million customers across North America, but it also owns the power plants spinning behind the grid. By running about 25 gigawatts of generation alongside its consumer retail brands, NRG captures a margin on the wholesale megawatt and another margin on the customer's living-room switch.

That dual model puts the company squarely inside the artificial intelligence power crunch. Large language models require around-the-clock baseload electricity, making dispatchable natural gas the primary bottleneck for data centers trying to plug into an overloaded grid.

Yet the AI power trade spent early November hitting a wall. Fears of a sudden data-center slowdown emerged after strategists warned that roughly 30% of expected 2028 data-center additions were at risk. Sector shares tumbled, pulling NRG down roughly 16% across two sessions before the stock found its footing.

Against that market rout, the utility delivered a blowout quarter. In its third-quarter earnings release, adjusted earnings per share jumped 68% year over year to $4.68, beating Wall Street consensus estimates by roughly 40%.

Adjusted EBITDA climbed 67% to surpass two billion dollars, lifted by wider retail margins during a hot Texas summer and rising East Coast capacity prices. Free cash flow before growth investments grew 50% to hit $1.24 billion.

The headline move, however, was a four-billion-dollar cash agreement to sell six natural-gas power plants back to LS Power, the private generation developer. The transaction sheds 4.9 gigawatts of generation across New York, New England, and Texas at an implied valuation of eight times forward EBITDA.

NRG retains its entire Mid-Atlantic fleet and its CPower commercial demand-response network, leaving the company with 20 gigawatts of generation split evenly between Texas and the East Coast.

The deal marks a remarkably swift trade. Back in January, NRG acquired 13 gigawatts of generation and CPower from LS Power in a twelve-billion-dollar transaction, issuing 24.25 million shares to the seller at a valuation well into the triple digits. Eleven months later, NRG is handing back about a third of that capacity for cash and using the proceeds to retire its own shares at a discount.

In a sector obsessed with hoarding generation, NRG is treating power plants like liquid inventory and its own stock as the mispriced asset.

The cash windfall fuels an aggressive capital return program. Management plans to execute three billion dollars in share repurchases across 2026 and 2027, starting with an extra billion-dollar buyback tranche before the end of the fourth quarter. Another three billion dollars will retire debt to keep leverage flat, while the annualized dividend rises 8% to $2.05 per share.

For the equity to re-rate, the company must prove that shrinking its physical footprint actually boosts per-share earnings. Shares currently trade around nine times forward consensus earnings, while equity analysts maintain a consensus price target roughly 70% above the current price. An updated financial model following the expected mid-2027 close needs to show that aggressive share retirement outweighs the lost earnings from the divested turbines.

The bear case sees a utility cannibalizing its earnings engine just as growth stalls out. Initial 2027 guidance calls for an adjusted earnings midpoint of $9.05 per share—less than 2% higher than 2026—and that projection does not yet deduct the earnings lost from the six divested plants.

Management's long-term plan assumes regional wholesale power prices between $52 and $53 per megawatt-hour, but the CFO conceded on the third-quarter earnings call that Texas forward prices for 2027 already sit below that estimate. If wholesale power prices stay weak or hyperscalers balk at signing on-site contracts, NRG is simply a smaller company with $148 million in unrestricted cash and a heavy debt load.

The missing commercial catalyst is the company's Bring Your Own Power initiative. The program plans to build 1.2 gigawatts of new gas generation placed directly beside customer data centers, bypassing multi-year interconnection queues with capital underwritten by the buyer.

What we are watching is whether NRG secures a signed definitive agreement for that project before December 31, 2026. A finalized contract would give the market a tangible dollar valuation for a pipeline it currently values at zero.

NRG has concluded that retiring its own discounted equity creates more value than owning extra turbines.

Disclosure: The Signal holds no position in NRG. Positions may change. This is not financial advice.
